title: What is the best practice to declare and initialize in __init__ function?
author: sgwzq
duncathan
text: This looks like a problem which may be served by use of descriptors. Possibly just by using @property. Have you looked into either of those?

author: petercordia
text:
It looks like you’re trying to force attribute protection onto Python. Perhaps you’re coming from a language where this is common, and it makes you feel comfortable?
I would encourage you to try the ‘pythonic’ paradigm: no protection at all
class MyClass:
  def __init__(self, var):
    self.var = var

I understand depending on your background something in you may initially protest against this. But consider how this class is going to be used. Only by yourself? Then agree with yourself some conduct that will ensure that MyClass.var will only be changed appropriately. Only within this repository, but by a team you need to work together with? Then agree on such a conduct with your team. Most teams already have such a conduct. (Even if it usually isn’t explicit.)
Is this a library, and you feel the need to protect yourself for the sake of inheritance by other people you have no relation with? Design the interface with the user so that they don’t need inheritance. And use a @final decorator if it makes you feel better.
As I said, I understand this can feel weird. But sincerely, give it a try before you dismiss it.

author: svioletg
text:
I’m sort of unclear on what your ultimate goal is with the code snippets given, but as one suggestion, if you want to be explicit about what attributes are allowed to be defined/assigned on your class and want to enforce that, you can use the __slots__ attribute like so:
class A:
    __slots__ = ('x', 'y')
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

Which will raise an error at runtime if you try to define any attribute on an instance of A that isn’t in A.__slots__:
In [1]: class A:
   ...:     __slots__ = ('x', 'y')
   ...:     def __init__(self, x, y):
   ...:         self.x = x
   ...:         self.y = y
   ...:

In [2]: a = A(1, 2)

In [3]: a.x = 1

In [4]: a.y = 2

In [5]: a.z = 3
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
AttributeError                            Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[5], line 1
----> 1 a.z = 3

AttributeError: 'A' object has no attribute 'z'

author: roelschroeven
sgwzq
text:
Thank you for your elaborated answer. Maybe because I’m not a native English speaker and my description is not accurate.  I apologize for that.
I know the advantages of OOP. It packs all of the related data and methods into a class so that when another one invokes setter function, all of the fast, unimportant, and trivial process are handled implicitly and automatically. Such properties enable better encapsulation, and many client-oriented projects need this.
My class is indeed mutable, and your answer does enlighten me. I could turn a OOP language into a structured program in this way. But as you might have understood, the biggest difficulties are from merging these styles together. And what’s even worse is that different people adopts different logic when contributing to the same open-source project.
I think I’d better describe the backgrounds of what I’m doing. Users will enter a structure of a molecule. It contains all of the XYZ coordinates of nuclei of a molecule. e.g. For a water molecule, it looks like
mol = Mole()
mol.atom = '''
    O 0 0 0;
    H 0  0.748 0.584;
    H 0 -0.748 0.584
    '''
mol.temperature = 298.15 # Just as an example
mol.pressure = 1

And instant information, such as num_of_electrons, num_of_cores could be easily calculated when we change any of these attributes. This looks like the Line instance above.
A user wants to know detailed information. e.g. electron_density_around_atoms matrix attribute. And this is assigned from the most time consuming part of a scientific program. We do that by labor-intensive calculations. They include integrals of spacial functions of an electron when we want to calculate how much every two electrons interacts. And it also includes iteration, because the current algorithm follows such a self-consistent procedure.
1. Guess the approximate potential around the molecule

2. For electrons 1 to 10, calculate their own orbitals accordingly
3. Calculate the potential generated by these rough orbitals
4. Check if this potential varies from the last potential. 
    If so, terminate, otherwise, loop back to step 2.

In conclusion, the number of total complexity is about O(N^4). Very expensive.
Maybe I have written too much. But I appreciate it if you understand me. I’d say, we cannot re calc immediately after num_of_electrons change, instead, after all variables are set, do.
So, this sounds like neither structural programming nor object-oriented programming. It is the combination of both. Neither of the styles are perfect for me. It isn’t following the simple OOP style.
The step 2 and step 3 could be divided into many subroutines. And these takes up most of proportion of methods in this class. They sometimes share some common intermediate variables, but these intermediate variables are continuously updating and NOT important for the final result. So it is troublesome whether to parse them as arguments (not important variable and make the subroutine argument list complex)  or to save it as instance attribute (big, continuously updating, and not important for final results). It also matters whether I employ assigning self. attributes from getters after returning from subroutines strategy or the updating self. attributes from subroutines one.
Do you feel exhausted now? I do, so that’s why I’m asking here. And that’s the reason why many people are still using Fortran. Some of them don’t want to try OOP at all. What they write may be not reusable either.

author: duncathan
sgwzq
text:
Dunc Graham:

need to calculate it at all until the user needs it? Rather than calculating proactively, you could


Do you mean, to invoke all of the calculating functions manually? It is a good strategy. And originally I thought a class should be written like this. Just a lot of getter function will help me do that. Until I read The Pragmatic Programmer, which told me a concise way like this:
 class myclass:
    def __init__(self, object_):
        # declaration and assignment
        self.__varA = None
        self.__varB = None
        self.__varC = None # B and C are consequential vars from A. e.g. C = A + B
        self.__updateA(init_value)
        
    def calc_then_reset(self, another_obj, options):
        results = xxx
        self.__updateA(results)

    def __updateA(self, results)
        self.__varA = xxx
        __updateB(self.__varA)

    def __updateB(self, varA)
        self.__varB = xxx
        __updateC(self.__varB)

    def __updateC(self, varB)
        self.__varC = xxx


Maybe I shouldn’t have read the book, but it did inspire me why to embrace OOP. It omitted the duplicated updating process in calc_then_reset (and there may be many calc_then_reset functions, where only __updateAs are needed). Maybe I shouldn’t have known that… 
I don’t know whether this sounds pythonic. And I’m really grateful if you can share your opinions.
Thank you!

author: sgwzq
text:
I would like the user to have the least manual settings.
That’s to say, immediately after he inputs the atoms, all of the other attributes are updated automatically. So I think setters and updaters should exist, just like when we insert a stack frame to a stack, the total number of elements increments with no need of manual intervention.
However, just as you found above, some of the procedures are too expensive. And these needs to be reserved for the user to do manually. After he feels he sets all good parameters, he will run the expensive part.
This could be a mix between structural programming and object-oriented programming. And definitely, if we want the user to intervene and operate less, the program gets complicated.
Some of the variables should follow the automatically updated routine, and if all attributes are of this type, we could simply structure the program using setters and getters. A user can freely update any attributes, and get any other ones at any time precisely.
But some other ones follow the structured programming. i.e. This kind of programs are sequential, Running from head to end without backward checking.  The user may get a correct result when he only invokes the num_electrons once. He will have a wrong result if he inits the class, asks for the num_electrons, changes the atom attribute, and asks again.
It is complicated, but I think it is inevitable. Thank you for your effort to discuss with me.
